title: The Night He Was Handed Over
sum: Jesus has finished his teaching. Now he tells his disciples that in two days, at Passover, the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified. While the chief priests plot, a woman pours costly oil on his head in Bethany, and Jesus says she has prepared him for burial. Judas goes to the priests and agrees to hand him over for thirty silver coins.

At the Passover meal Jesus names his betrayer, then takes bread and a cup and gives them new meaning: "This is my body," "this is my blood of the covenant... so that sins can be forgiven." In Gethsemane he prays three times to be spared the cup, and three times finds his friends asleep. Judas arrives with a crowd and a kiss; the disciples flee. Before the high priest, Jesus is charged with threatening the sanctuary and, under oath, says he will be seen at God's right hand. The council finds him guilty of blasphemy. Outside, Peter denies him three times and weeps.

The chapter is built on contrasts: the woman's love and Judas's greed, Jesus' watchfulness and the disciples' sleep, Jesus' truth under oath and Peter's lies under oath. Below are deep dives on the Last Supper, the trial, and Gethsemane.
readings: Most historians agree that Jesus shared a final meal with his disciples, was arrested at night near the Mount of Olives with the help of an insider, was questioned by the high priest Caiaphas, and was handed to Pilate. They debate the date of the meal (see 26:17), the legality and nature of the hearing (see 26:59), and how much of the dialogue anyone could have reported.

Matthew follows Mark closely but sharpens it. Jesus is in command throughout: he announces the date (26:2), names the traitor (26:25), sets the place (26:18), and tells Judas to get on with it (26:50). Matthew alone gives the thirty coins, Judas's "It isn't me, is it, Rabbi?", the word about the sword and the twelve legions, and "from now on." Every step happens "so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled" (26:56).

From the earliest days Christians have relived this chapter in worship. The words over the bread and cup are spoken at every Eucharist, Mass, Divine Liturgy or Lord's Supper; Paul quotes a form of them in the 50s (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). Holy Thursday or Maundy Thursday keeps the night of the Supper, Gethsemane is the model of Christian prayer in anguish, and Peter's tears the model of repentance.

views.H: The plot, the arrest and the hearing fit what is known of Jerusalem under Caiaphas and Pilate: leaders who feared riots at Passover (Josephus tells of several), a high priest who kept office by cooperating with Rome, and a Galilean prophet whose action in the Temple days before (21:12–13) threatened public order. The night arrest outside the city avoided the crowds. Whether the meal was the Passover itself is debated (see the deep dive).
views.C: Matthew rewrites Mark 14 with small but telling changes: "eat" added to the bread word, "for the forgiveness of sins" added to the cup word (and taken away from John's baptism, 3:1–12), Judas's question, "from now on" in 26:64, and the agreement with Luke against Mark at 26:68 that fuels the debate over Q. Many scholars hold that the words of institution were shaped by worship before any Gospel was written; Paul's version (1 Corinthians 11:23–25) is the earliest written form.
views.L: The chapter is framed by Jesus' prediction that he will be handed over to be crucified (26:2) and Peter's tears after his denial (26:75). Three times Jesus prays and three times the disciples sleep; three times Peter denies. Matthew sets Jesus' truthful answer under oath (26:63–64) and Peter's false oath (26:72) side by side, in two rooms of the same house. The Lord's Prayer (6:9–13) is prayed in Gethsemane.
views.J: Jesus is a Jew keeping Passover with Jewish friends, using the blessings over bread and wine, singing the Hallel, and praying to God as "my Father" in words close to Jewish prayer. Jewish scholars such as Geza Vermes, Paula Fredriksen and Amy-Jill Levine stress that the hostility in the story belongs to a small priestly elite in a tense political setting, not to the Jewish people, and that the trial as Matthew tells it conflicts with later Jewish law (the Mishnah), though the Mishnah may not show the rules of AD 30.
views.T: The church fathers read the chapter sacramentally and morally: the anointing as Christ's kingship, the Supper as the institution of the Eucharist, Gethsemane as proof that Christ had a true human soul and will (Maximus the Confessor; the Third Council of Constantinople, 681), Peter as the model of repentance and Judas of despair. Holy Week liturgies in East and West read this chapter, and the Orthodox call this night "the betrayal."

deep.h: The Last Supper: Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul
deep.b:
Four early accounts give the words over the bread and the cup, in two families:

  • Mark 14:22–24 and Matthew 26:26–28: "This is my body" / "This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many." Matthew adds "eat," "drink from it, all of you," and "so that sins can be forgiven."
  • Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:23–25 and Luke 22:19–20: "This is my body, which is being given for you. Do this to remember me" / "This cup is the new covenant, made in my blood" (Luke's wording; Paul's is almost the same). Paul's letter, written in the mid-50s, is the oldest written account.

All four agree on the core: Jesus took bread and a cup at a final meal, linked them with his body and his blood, and spoke of a covenant. The words echo Exodus 24:8 (the blood of the covenant at Sinai), Jeremiah 31:31 (the new covenant), and Isaiah 53:12 (the servant who bore the sin of many). Matthew does not have "do this in remembrance of me"; for him the meal is part of Jesus' last night, told as the founding of what the church already did. On how Christians understand "This is my body," see the Where Christians differ cards below.

Matthew, Mark and Luke clearly call it the Passover (26:17–19). John places Jesus' death on the afternoon before the Passover meal, when the lambs were slaughtered (John 18:28; 19:14, 31). Joachim Jeremias listed features that fit a Passover: a meal at night inside Jerusalem, reclining, wine, a hymn at the end, words explaining the food. Others point out that the accounts never mention the lamb or bitter herbs, and that a Sanhedrin hearing and an execution on the feast day itself would be strange. Proposals include John's theological dating (Jesus as the lamb), a different calendar used by some groups (Annie Jaubert), or a farewell meal held the night before Passover with Passover themes. Astronomers have tried to date the full moons: 14 Nisan fell on a Friday in AD 30 and AD 33, which fits John's dating, though ancient calendars depended on sighting the new moon and cannot be fixed with certainty.

Matthew presents a night session of "the entire Sanhedrin" seeking false testimony, two witnesses about the sanctuary, the high priest's oath, Jesus' answer from Psalm 110 and Daniel 7, the charge of blasphemy, and a verdict of death. Historians weigh it in three ways:

  • A formal but illegal trial. The Mishnah's tractate Sanhedrin forbids capital trials at night or before a festival and requires a second day for a guilty verdict. On this view the leaders broke their own rules, and the illegality is part of the story's point.
  • A trial under different rules. The Mishnah was written down around AD 200 by sages in the Pharisees' tradition and describes an ideal court. The Sadducean high priests of AD 30 may have worked differently.
  • A hearing, not a trial. John 18:13–24 describes questioning by Annas and Caiaphas, and Luke 22:66 places a council meeting in the morning. The night session may have been an inquiry to frame a charge for Pilate, the only one who could order a crucifixion.

Raymond Brown's The Death of the Messiah remains the fullest study. Whatever its form, the gospels agree that the high priest's circle, not the Jewish people, handed Jesus to Pilate, and that Pilate gave the order.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two oaths in one house
deep.b: Matthew alone stresses oaths in this chapter: the high priest puts Jesus "under oath" by the living God (26:63), and Peter denies "with an oath" and then with curses (26:72, 74). In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus told his followers not to swear but to let their yes be yes and their no be no (5:33–37). My suggestion is that Matthew arranges the two scenes as a lesson on that teaching. Jesus, forced under oath, does not swear at all; he answers with a guarded yes, "You said it," and then tells the truth plainly. Peter, not forced to swear, piles up oaths to support a lie. The one who keeps 5:37 is condemned; the one who breaks it walks free and weeps. Commentators such as Davies and Allison note the link between 26:72 and 5:33–37; I am proposing that Matthew meant the two scenes as a deliberate pair.

echoes: Exodus 12; Exodus 24:8; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Zechariah 11:12–13; Zechariah 13:7; Isaiah 53:7–12; Psalm 41:9; Psalm 42:5; Psalm 110:1; Daniel 7:13–14; Mark 14:1–72; Luke 22:1–71; John 12:1–8; John 13:1–30; John 18:1–27; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26

settings.what: Jesus foretells his death at Passover
settings.to: his disciples, on the Mount of Olives
settings.when: two days before Passover, at the end of his last long speech (chapters 24–25)
settings.why: to tell them plainly that the next event is his own death, and that it will come at the feast that remembers Israel's rescue
settings.readers: Matthew's community, which kept the Lord's Supper and probably still knew Passover, learned to read Jesus' death through the feast of freedom.

settings.by: the chief priests and the people's elders
settings.to: one another, in the courtyard of Caiaphas
settings.when: the same days, with Jerusalem full of pilgrims
settings.why: to agree on removing Jesus quietly, while avoiding an uproar among the festival crowds that admired him
settings.readers: If, as most critical scholars think, Matthew wrote after AD 70, when the high priesthood had fallen, the scene explained to his readers who had opposed Jesus and why; the plot belongs to a leadership group, not to the people they feared.

settings.what: Jesus defends the woman who anointed him
settings.to: the disciples, who had complained of waste, at dinner in Simon's house in Bethany
settings.when: days before Passover
settings.why: to correct the disciples and to give her act its meaning: preparation for his burial, to be told wherever the good news goes
settings.readers: The church that told the story fulfilled the promise each time it did so, and learned that devotion to Jesus is not waste.

settings.to: the chief priests
settings.when: after the anointing at Bethany
settings.why: to sell the priests the moment of arrest: Judas offers to hand Jesus over at a quiet time, away from the crowds, and the priests pay thirty silver coins, the price of a slave in Exodus 21:32
settings.readers: Matthew's readers would hear Zechariah 11 and the price of a slave, and see that betrayal came from inside the circle of the Twelve.

settings.to: the disciples, and through them an unnamed host in Jerusalem
settings.when: the first day of Unleavened Bread
settings.why: to arrange the meal, with Jesus fixing the time as "my time"
settings.readers: The secrecy and Jesus' command of the arrangements told readers that nothing that followed caught him by surprise.

settings.to: the Twelve at the Passover table, and Judas in particular
settings.when: during the meal
settings.why: to show that he knows, to give Judas a last chance, and to declare both God's plan and Judas's guilt
settings.readers: For Matthew's community, a warning that sharing the Lord's table does not guarantee loyalty.

settings.what: The words over the bread and the cup
settings.to: the twelve disciples at the Passover table
settings.when: during the meal, on his last night
settings.why: to give his coming death its meaning, as the covenant sacrifice that brings forgiveness, and to bind his followers to him in a meal they would repeat until the kingdom comes
settings.readers: Matthew's church already celebrated the Lord's Supper. The scene told them where their meal came from and what it meant; the words may already have been shaped by their worship.
views: Jesus reinterpreted the Passover's bread and cup (Jeremias, most of the church).
A last meal before Passover, given Passover meaning (many historians, following John's dating).

settings.what: Jesus foretells desertion and Peter's denial
settings.to: the disciples, on the way to the Mount of Olives
settings.when: after the hymn, that night
settings.why: to warn them that they will all fall, using Zechariah 13:7, and to promise that he will meet them again in Galilee
settings.readers: The story of the leaders' failure, kept in their own church, taught later disciples humility and hope after failure.

settings.to: the disciples, told to sit while he prays; his Father, three times; and Peter, James and John, who sleep
settings.when: late that night, in the olive grove
settings.why: to pray for the cup to pass and to submit to the Father's will, and to urge his friends to watch and pray against testing
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, facing persecution (10:17–22; 24:9), saw how to pray in anguish: honestly, and with "may your will be done."

settings.to: Judas; the disciple who drew a sword; and the crowds sent by the priests
settings.when: at the moment of arrest
settings.why: to refuse violence and angelic rescue, and to tell the crowds that the Scriptures are being fulfilled
settings.readers: For a church living under Rome, and perhaps, if Matthew wrote after AD 70, after a failed Jewish war, a clear word that Jesus' kingdom does not come by the sword.

settings.what: The hearing before the high priest
settings.by: false witnesses, the high priest Caiaphas, and Jesus
settings.to: the Sanhedrin, gathered in the high priest's house
settings.when: that night
settings.why: the council seeks grounds for death; the high priest puts Jesus under oath; Jesus answers with Psalm 110 and Daniel 7 that he will be vindicated by God
settings.readers: Matthew's readers heard Jesus' confession as their own: the condemned Jesus is the Son of Man who will judge, already at God's right hand.
views: A full trial by the council, illegal by later Jewish rules.
An inquiry to frame a charge for Pilate (Brown, Sanders).

settings.by: Peter, answering two slave girls and the bystanders
settings.to: servants and officers in the high priest's courtyard
settings.when: while Jesus was being questioned inside
settings.why: Peter tries to save himself; the scene shows the cost of the fear Jesus had warned of
settings.readers: A church that met under pressure to deny Christ (compare Pliny's letter about cursing Christ) found in Peter both a warning and a hope.

traditions.q: Jesus said "This is my body" and "This is my blood" (26:26–28). Is Christ's body and blood truly present in the bread and wine?
views: Yes. By the priest's words of consecration the whole substance of the bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation), while the appearances remain. Christ is present "truly, really, and substantially," and the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the cross (Council of Trent, Session 13; Catechism 1374–1377).

Yes. The bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood when the Holy Spirit is called down in the liturgy (the epiclesis). Modern Orthodox teachers usually prefer not to define how, calling it a mystery and using the word "change" (metabolē). But the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 (the Confession of Dositheus, decree 17) did use the word metousiōsis, the Greek for transubstantiation.

Yes. Christ's true body and blood are present "in, with, and under" the bread and wine and are received by all who eat, by believers for blessing and unbelievers for judgment. Lutherans reject transubstantiation and insist on the plain word "is" (Augsburg Confession X; Formula of Concord VII; Luther's catechisms).

Christ is truly present, but spiritually: his body is in heaven, and by the Holy Spirit believers are lifted up to feed on him by faith. The bread and wine are signs and seals, not changed (Calvin, Institutes 4.17; Westminster Confession 29). Zwingli, an early Reformed leader, held a more symbolic view.

The Thirty-Nine Articles reject transubstantiation and teach that "the Body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten, in the Supper, only after an heavenly and spiritual manner" by faith (Article 28). Anglicans range from Anglo-Catholics who hold a real objective presence to evangelicals close to the Reformed view.

Methodism's Articles of Religion (Article 18) keep the Anglican wording that Christ's body is received "only after a heavenly and spiritual manner" and reject transubstantiation. John and Charles Wesley's Hymns on the Lord's Supper (1745) speak warmly of Christ's real presence and of the Supper as a means of grace, without defining how.

The Supper is an ordinance, not a sacrament: a symbolic act of obedience in which believers remember Christ's death and anticipate his return. The bread and wine represent his body and blood and are not changed (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 7; Second London Confession 30, which keeps a Calvinist "spiritual" feeding).

traditions.q: Jesus said of the cup, "Every one of you, drink from it" (26:27). Must all who receive communion be given the cup as well as the bread?
views: The words "Every one of you, drink from it" were spoken to the apostles at the Last Supper, not as a command that every believer must receive the cup (Council of Trent, Session 21, chapter 1). The whole Christ is received under either form alone, so communion under the bread only is valid. For centuries the cup was reserved to the priest in the West; since the Second Vatican Council the cup may be offered to the people, and often is, but it is not required (Council of Trent, Session 21; Catechism 1390).
Everyone receives both: the bread is placed in the cup and given with a spoon, to all the baptized, including infants.
Both kinds must be given to all, because Christ commanded "drink from it, all of you"; withholding the cup is against his institution (Augsburg Confession XXII).
"The Cup of the Lord is not to be denied to the Lay-people: for both the parts of the Lord's Sacrament... ought to be ministered to all Christian men alike" (Article 30).
Both elements are given to all communicants as Christ commanded; denying the cup to the people is rejected (Westminster Confession 29.4).

traditions.q: Jesus stopped a disciple who drew a sword to defend him: "Everyone who takes the sword will be destroyed by the sword" (26:52). Does this forbid force even to defend the innocent, or only private violence for Christ's cause? (The wider question of war and military service is on the card at 5:39.)
views: It forbids the sword to Christians altogether. If the disciple could not use it to defend the innocent Son of God, a believer may not use it to defend himself or the faith (Schleitheim Confession, article 6). Quakers read the verse the same way.

It condemns taking up the sword on one's own authority. Aquinas explains "takes the sword" as using it without lawful authority (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 40, article 1). Defending oneself or others with proportionate force remains lawful and can be a duty (Catechism 2263–2265).

Peter acted as a private person and for the gospel, which is not spread or defended by force; the verse does not take the sword from the government (Luther, Temporal Authority; Augsburg Confession XVI).
Jesus rebuked a private act that also resisted God's plan for the cross; the lawful magistrate still bears the sword (Westminster Confession 23.2).

title: The King on the Cross
sum: At dawn the leaders hand Jesus over to Pilate. Judas, seeing Jesus condemned, regrets it, throws the silver into the sanctuary and hangs himself; the priests buy a potter's field with the money, which Matthew reads as a fulfilled prophecy. Before Pilate, Jesus says almost nothing. Pilate offers the crowd a choice between Jesus Barabbas and Jesus called the Messiah. His wife warns him about "that righteous man" after a dream. The crowd, persuaded by the chief priests, calls for crucifixion. Pilate washes his hands, and "all the people" answer, "His blood on us, and on our children!"

Roman soldiers crown Jesus with thorns and mock him as king. Simon of Cyrene carries his cross to Golgotha. Under a placard reading "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews," between two bandits, he is mocked in the words of Psalm 22. Darkness covers the land; at three o'clock he cries, "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" and dies. The sanctuary curtain tears, the earth shakes, tombs open, and the Roman guard confesses, "This man really was God's Son!" Women from Galilee watch. Joseph of Arimathea buries him in his own tomb, and the chief priests and Pharisees have it sealed and guarded.

No chapter of Matthew has been read with more devotion, and none has been more misused. The deep dives below cover "His blood on us," Pilate and the question of responsibility, and the signs at Jesus' death.
readings: That Jesus was crucified by order of Pontius Pilate is among the most secure facts of ancient history, confirmed by Tacitus and Josephus. Historians weigh other details differently: the Barabbas custom (not attested outside the Gospels), Pilate's reluctance (which fits some accounts of his politics but not Philo's portrait of a brutal governor), the scenes only Matthew tells (Judas's death, the dream, the hand-washing, the raised saints, the guard), and the role of the crowd.

Matthew presents the crucifixion as an enthronement. Jesus is anointed (26:7), robed, crowned and hailed as king (27:28–29), lifted up under a royal title (27:37) with men at his right and left (27:38), and confessed as God's Son by Gentiles (27:54). Every detail fulfills Scripture: Zechariah, Psalm 22, Psalm 69, Isaiah 53. The cosmic signs show that his death is the turning of the ages.

From the second century on, Christians read 27:25 as Israel's self-curse, and the chapter was preached on Good Friday in ways that led to violence against Jews. Since the Holocaust, churches and scholars have reread it in its first-century setting and rejected the charge of deicide against the Jewish people. Reading the chapter honestly today means knowing both its meaning for Matthew and what was done with it.

views.H: Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves, bandits and rebels against Roman rule; the charge "King of the Jews" is political. Pilate governed from AD 26 to 36 and is known from Philo, Josephus, Tacitus and the Pilate stone. Jewish leaders could bring an accusation; only the governor could crucify. Simon of Cyrene, Joseph of Arimathea and the women are named witnesses. The darkness, the earthquake and the raised saints have no outside confirmation.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 15 and adds a cluster of scenes found in no other Gospel: Judas's death (27:3–10), Pilate's wife (27:19), the hand-washing and the people's cry (27:24–25), the earthquake and the raised saints (27:51–53), and the guard (27:62–66). Many critical scholars see in these additions Matthew's apologetic and polemical concerns after AD 70: answering the stolen-body charge, showing Jesus' innocence, and laying blame on the leaders and "all the people" of the generation that saw Jerusalem fall.
views.L: Blood is the chapter's thread (27:4, 6, 8, 24, 25), echoing 23:35 and 26:28. The trial before Pilate mirrors the trial before Caiaphas: silence, a question about identity, a guarded answer, mockery. The mockery at the cross repeats the devil's "if you are the Son of God" (4:3, 6; 27:40). The Gentiles at the edges, Pilate's wife and the centurion, see what the leaders do not.
views.J: Jewish readers have known this chapter mainly through what it led to: the charge that Jews killed God, Good Friday violence, and blood libels. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine and Paula Fredriksen read 27:25 as Matthew's polemic in a quarrel within the Jewish family after AD 70, place the responsibility for the crucifixion on Rome and a small priestly group, and note that the crowd at Pilate's residence could not speak for all Jews. Jesus, his family, his disciples and the women at the cross were Jews; so was Matthew.
views.T: The church fathers read the chapter through the creed: "crucified under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried." They saw the cross as Christ's throne, the torn curtain as the opening of heaven, the raised saints as the beginning of Christ's victory over Hades. Many also read 27:25 as a curse on the Jews (Origen, Chrysostom). The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate (1965) and many Protestant and Orthodox statements since have rejected collective Jewish guilt, while the Catechism stresses that sinners, all of them, bear responsibility for Christ's death (Catechism 597–598).

deep.h: "His blood on us, and on our children" (27:25): meaning and misuse
deep.b:
What the words meant. The cry uses a biblical formula for accepting responsibility for a death: "his blood will be on his own head" (Joshua 2:19); "Your blood is on your head" (2 Samuel 1:16). Pilate has just declared himself "clean" of the blood; the crowd takes it on. In Matthew's plot the crowd is persuaded by the chief priests (27:20). If, as most critical scholars think, Matthew wrote after the Romans burned the Temple in AD 70, "our children" probably meant the next generation, the one that saw Jerusalem fall, which Jesus had warned in 23:35–36 ("all this will come on this generation"). Many scholars, Ulrich Luz among them, think Matthew saw the city's destruction as the consequence of this moment; that is a judgment on one generation, not a curse on all Jews forever.

A double meaning? In Matthew, Jesus' blood is "poured out for many, so that sins can be forgiven" (26:28). Some interpreters, including Timothy Cargal and Pope Benedict XVI (Jesus of Nazareth: Holy Week, 2011), read the cry as unwittingly asking for that blood: Jesus' blood does not cry out for vengeance like Abel's but for reconciliation (Hebrews 12:24).

How it was used. From the early church on, the verse was read as Israel's self-curse. Melito of Sardis (about 170) accused Israel of murdering God. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Matthew (86), read the cry as bringing ruin on the people and their children, and his sermons against Judaizing Christians (386–387) attacked Jews with savage force. In the Middle Ages it was cited in sermons, passion plays and at Easter riots, and it fed the charge of "Christ-killers" behind massacres, expulsions and blood libels. Martin Luther's On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) drew on this tradition, and the Nazis exploited it, as the historian Jules Isaac showed in The Teaching of Contempt.

The churches' response. The Second Vatican Council declared that what happened in the passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today," and that Jews should not be presented "as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures" (Nostra Aetate 4, 1965). The Catechism teaches that "all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion," repeating the sixteenth-century Roman Catechism (Catechism 597–598). The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) repudiated Luther's anti-Jewish writings, and many other churches have made similar statements. Jewish scholars responded in Dabru Emet (2000), which affirmed that Christians and Jews worship the same God, and also argued that Nazism was not an inevitable outcome of Christianity, though centuries of Christian anti-Judaism helped make it possible.

This translation keeps the verse exactly as the Greek has it. The text should not be softened; neither should its history.

deep.h: Who was responsible for Jesus' death?
deep.b:
The Gospels name several parties: Judas, who handed him over; the chief priests and elders, who wanted him dead; the crowd at the governor's residence; Pilate, who gave the order; and Roman soldiers, who carried it out. Historians agree on the essentials: Jesus was executed by a Roman governor in a Roman way on a political charge, after the high priest's circle handed him over. The Gospels' tendency to show Pilate as reluctant has been read as an apology to Rome by Christians who lived under its power. Philo and Josephus describe Pilate as harsh, which makes his hesitation surprising, though a governor might still resist being pressured by local leaders.

Theologically, the New Testament gives a wider answer: Jesus was handed over "by God's set purpose" (Acts 2:23), he gave himself (20:28), and he died "for our sins" (1 Corinthians 15:3). Christian tradition from the Roman Catechism of 1566 on has taught that every sinner shares the guilt, and hymns such as "Ah, holy Jesus" ("I crucified thee") put it in the first person.

Matthew gives more signs than any other Gospel: darkness from noon to three (with Mark and Luke), the torn curtain (with Mark and Luke), and, his alone, an earthquake, split rocks, opened tombs, and saints raised who later appear in Jerusalem. These are the signs the prophets linked to the Day of the Lord and the resurrection of the dead: darkness at noon (Amos 8:9), the earth shaking (Joel 2:10), graves opened (Ezekiel 37:12–13), the Lord standing on the Mount of Olives with his holy ones (Zechariah 14:4–5). Matthew presents Jesus' death as the moment when the end of the age breaks in.

Readers differ on how to take them. Most of the church has read them as events. Many modern scholars, including some evangelicals, read the raised saints as an apocalyptic image, a way of saying that Jesus' death opens the graves. No ancient writer outside the Gospels mentions them. Matthew's own wording is restrained: the saints appear "to many," not to everyone, and are not mentioned again.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three people who see what the leaders miss
deep.b: Matthew sets three outsiders around the cross who recognize Jesus while Israel's leaders reject him: Pilate's wife, a Gentile woman who calls him "righteous" after a dream (27:19); the centurion and his men, Gentile soldiers who call him "God's Son" (27:54); and Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man, the kind Jesus said could hardly enter the kingdom, who becomes his disciple (27:57). Each of the three matches an unlikely group from Matthew's opening chapters: the dreams given to Joseph and the magi (1:20; 2:12), the Gentile magi who worship the king (2:11), and the costly gifts of the wealthy from the east (2:11). My suggestion is that Matthew framed the passion to answer the infancy story: as at the birth, outsiders recognize the king while Jerusalem's rulers seek his death (2:3–4, 16). Scholars have long noted the link between "King of the Jews" in 2:2 and 27:37; the threefold parallel I propose is my own.

echoes: Zechariah 11:12–13; Jeremiah 18–19; Jeremiah 32:6–15; Deuteronomy 21:6–9; 2 Samuel 1:16; Joshua 2:19; Psalm 22:1–18; Psalm 69:21; Isaiah 53:7–12; Amos 8:9; Ezekiel 37:12–13; Daniel 6:17; Mark 15:1–47; Luke 23:1–56; John 18:28–19:42; Acts 1:16–20

settings.what: Judas's confession and the priests' answer
settings.by: Judas; the chief priests and elders
settings.to: each other, at the Temple
settings.when: the morning Jesus was handed to Pilate
settings.why: Judas tries to undo his act by declaring Jesus innocent and returning the money; the priests refuse responsibility and turn the money to a burial field
settings.readers: Matthew's readers saw Jesus' innocence admitted by his betrayer, and a place name in Jerusalem, Field of Blood, explained by prophecy.

settings.to: Matthew's readers
settings.when: a comment on the purchase of the field
settings.why: to show that even the shameful price and its use were foreseen in Scripture
settings.readers: A Jewish-Christian community trained in Scripture would trace the links between Zechariah's shepherd and Jeremiah's potter and field.

settings.by: Pontius Pilate; the chief priests and elders as accusers
settings.to: Jesus
settings.when: early morning, at the governor's residence
settings.why: Pilate tests the political charge, "King of the Jews"; Jesus' silence fulfills Isaiah 53:7 and leaves the accusers to prove their case
settings.readers: Christians who would be brought before governors and kings (10:18) learned from Jesus' bearing.

settings.what: Barabbas or Jesus; the hand-washing; the people's cry (27:15–18, 20–26)
settings.by: Pilate, the chief priests and elders, the crowd
settings.to: the crowd gathered at the governor's judgment seat
settings.when: the Passover amnesty, that morning
settings.why: Pilate seeks a way out; the leaders win over the crowd; Pilate disclaims guilt; the crowd accepts it
settings.readers: If, as most critical scholars think, Matthew wrote after AD 70, his community could read the scene as explaining, in their terms, the fall of Jerusalem to the generation that rejected Jesus; scholars who date Matthew earlier read it as a warning. For later readers, a passage that must be read with its history of misuse in view.
views: "All the people" means everyone gathered there, a crowd stirred up by the leaders.
Matthew means the people of Israel as a whole at that moment, with consequences for that generation (Luz).

settings.to: Pilate, on the judge's bench
settings.when: during the hearing, that morning
settings.why: to warn him to have nothing to do with a man she calls righteous, because of what she suffered in a dream
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, who knew that God speaks through dreams in this Gospel (1:20; 2:12–22), heard a Gentile woman bear witness to Jesus' innocence while the leaders sought his death.

settings.by: the governor's soldiers, the whole cohort
settings.to: Jesus
settings.when: after the sentence, in the Praetorium
settings.why: to ridicule a would-be "King of the Jews" with a mock coronation
settings.readers: Readers saw the irony: Gentile soldiers acted out the truth they mocked.

settings.by: passers-by, the chief priests with scribes and elders, the two bandits
settings.to: Jesus on the cross
settings.when: during the crucifixion
settings.why: to shame him and to prove him false: if he were God's Son, God would rescue him
settings.readers: Matthew's readers heard Psalm 22 and the devil's testing in the taunts, and knew that refusing to save himself was the way he saved others.

settings.to: God; overheard by bystanders who thought he called Elijah
settings.when: about three in the afternoon, just before he died
settings.why: a prayer of anguish in the words of Psalm 22:1, a psalm that ends in rescue and praise
settings.readers: Jewish-Christian readers knew the whole psalm and heard both the abandonment and the hope.
views: Jesus bore the judgment due to sin (Luther, Calvin).
Citing the first line called up the psalm's ending of vindication.

settings.by: the centurion and the soldiers with him
settings.to: one another, at the cross
settings.when: after the earthquake
settings.why: terror at the signs turns into a confession of who Jesus is
settings.readers: For a community welcoming Gentiles, the first full confession after Jesus' death comes from Roman soldiers.

settings.by: the chief priests and the Pharisees
settings.to: Pilate
settings.when: the next day, the Sabbath
settings.why: to prevent a claim of resurrection by securing the tomb
settings.readers: Matthew's readers met the charge that the disciples stole the body (28:15); this scene answered it.

title: Raised, and With You Always
sum: At dawn after the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary go to see the tomb. An earthquake, an angel like lightning, a stone rolled away, guards frozen with fear: the angel tells the women that Jesus has been raised, as he said, and sends them to tell the disciples to meet him in Galilee. On the way Jesus himself meets them. They hold his feet and bow down before him, and he sends them to "my brothers."

Meanwhile the guards report to the chief priests, who pay them to say the disciples stole the body, a story Matthew says was still told in his day. The eleven go to the mountain in Galilee. They worship, though some waver. Jesus, given all authority in heaven and on earth, sends them to make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and teaching them all he commanded. He promises to be with them every day until the end of the age.

The short chapter gathers the whole Gospel together: the angel of the birth story returns, the mountain recalls Moses, the commission undoes the limit of 10:5–6, and "I am with you" answers "Immanuel" (1:23).
readings: Historians agree that Jesus' followers came to believe, very soon after his death, that God had raised him and that they had seen him (1 Corinthians 15:3–8, from the 50s, passing on earlier tradition). They differ on what lay behind that belief: a bodily resurrection and an empty tomb (N. T. Wright, many others), visions without a physical body (Gerd Lüdemann, Bart Ehrman), or questions history cannot settle (Dale Allison). Matthew's guard story and its sequel are found only in Matthew.
Read as the ending of Matthew's story

Matthew ends with an inclusio: the Gospel that began with "Immanuel, God with us" (1:23) closes with "I am with you every day." The king who was born to be worshiped by Gentiles (2:11) now sends his followers to all nations. The authority Jesus refused from the devil on a mountain (4:8–10) is given him by the Father on a mountain. The teaching of the five speeches becomes the content of the mission.
Read as a commission to the church

The Great Commission has shaped Christian mission more than any other passage. The modern missionary movement grew from it, as in William Carey's An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792). It is also the main text for baptism in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and one root of the doctrine of the Trinity.

views.H: The women's discovery of the empty tomb is in all four Gospels, which many historians count as early tradition because women were weak witnesses in that culture (Josephus, Antiquities 4.219). Matthew's guard story answers a charge that Justin Martyr still heard around AD 155. The appearances in Galilee (Matthew, Mark 16:7, John 21) and in Jerusalem (Luke, John 20) are hard to put in one sequence.
views.C: Matthew extends Mark, whose oldest text ends at 16:8 with the women afraid and silent. Matthew adds the earthquake and angel on the stone, the meeting with Jesus, the guards' bribe, and the commission. Many critical scholars see the commission's language, especially the triple name, as shaped by the church's baptismal practice (compare Didache 7:1); others see a genuine core in the risen Jesus' sending of his followers.
views.L: The chapter repeats "go" and "tell" (28:7, 8, 10, 11, 19), with two kinds of messengers: the women carrying the truth, the guards carrying a paid lie. Fear meets joy (28:8). The ending gathers Matthew's themes: mountains, the angel of the Lord, worship, doubt, authority, the nations, teaching, and God's presence.
views.J: "Among Jews right up to today" (28:15) shows Matthew's community at odds with the synagogue of its town. Jewish readers from Justin's Trypho to the medieval Toledot Yeshu told other stories of the empty tomb. Modern Jewish scholars such as Pinchas Lapide (who thought a resurrection possible as a Jewish event) and Geza Vermes discussed the claim seriously. Whether "all the nations" in 28:19 includes Israel matters for how Christians relate to Jews today.
views.T: The fathers read 28:19 as the clearest text of the Trinity in the Gospels and used it against Arians (Athanasius, Basil of Caesarea). The church's creeds follow its order: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The resurrection reading is the Gospel of Easter in many traditions, and 28:16–20 is read at ordinations, missions and baptisms.

deep.b:
The resurrection accounts agree on the core: on the first day of the week, women led by Mary Magdalene went to the tomb, found it empty, and heard from heavenly messengers that Jesus was alive; then Jesus appeared to his followers. They differ in many details:

  • Who went: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary (Matthew); they and Salome (Mark); they, Joanna and others (Luke); Mary Magdalene (John, though she says "we").
  • The messengers: one angel on the stone (Matthew); a young man inside (Mark); two men (Luke); two angels (John).
  • The appearances: to the women and then the eleven in Galilee (Matthew); none in Mark's oldest text; on the road to Emmaus and in Jerusalem (Luke); to Mary, the disciples in Jerusalem, Thomas, and by the lake (John). Paul lists Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James and all the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:5–7).

Some readers see harmonizable accounts told from different viewpoints, others independent traditions that grew in the telling. Nearly all agree that the differences show the accounts were not coordinated, and that the early church did not smooth them out.

deep.h: The Great Commission and the Trinity
deep.b:
Matthew 28:19 is the only place in the Gospels where Father, Son and Holy Spirit appear in one formula. The words "into the name" (singular) for three persons became a foundation for the doctrine that God is one in three. The Didache, about AD 100, already gives this formula for baptism (Didache 7:1), and Justin Martyr describes baptism "in the name of God the Father and Lord of the universe, and of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit" (First Apology 61). Acts describes baptism "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38; 10:48), which most churches read as describing whose baptism it was rather than the words spoken.

Every Greek manuscript and early translation of Matthew has the three names. F. C. Conybeare argued in 1901 that the original read "make disciples of all the nations in my name," the form Eusebius of Caesarea often quotes before 325. Textual critics have generally rejected this: Eusebius also quotes the full form, he paraphrased freely, and no manuscript supports the short text. The verse is not yet a full doctrine of the Trinity, which the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) worked out, but it puts the three names side by side as one.

When Jesus first sent the Twelve, he said, "Do not go off on a road to the Gentiles... Instead, go to the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost" (10:5–6). He told the Canaanite woman he was sent only to Israel (15:24). Now he sends the eleven to "all the nations." Readers explain the change as a turning point in salvation history: the mission to Israel first, then, after the cross and resurrection, to everyone (compare Romans 1:16, "first for the Jew and for the Greek as well"). Whether the mission to Israel continues is the debate behind "nations or Gentiles" in 28:19 (see the note). Most scholars, and most churches, hold that Israel is included.

settings.to: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, at the tomb
settings.when: dawn on the first day of the week
settings.why: to calm their fear, announce that Jesus has been raised as he said, show them the empty place, and send them to the disciples with the meeting in Galilee
settings.readers: Matthew's community heard the first Easter proclamation in its simplest form: "He has been raised, exactly as he said."

settings.to: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, on the road
settings.when: as they hurried from the tomb
settings.why: to greet them, accept their homage, and send them to the disciples, now called "my brothers"
settings.readers: The first witnesses and first messengers of the resurrection are women; a church that read this knew where its message began.

settings.what: The bribe and the cover story
settings.by: the guards report; the chief priests and elders instruct them
settings.to: the soldiers, and through them the people
settings.when: the same morning
settings.why: to explain away the empty tomb with a claim of theft, and to protect the soldiers from the governor
settings.readers: Matthew addresses a story "among Jews right up to today," so his readers would know what to answer when they heard it.

settings.to: the eleven disciples, some still wavering, on a mountain in Galilee
settings.when: after the resurrection, at the place he had appointed
settings.why: to claim all authority, send them to make disciples of all nations by baptizing and teaching, and promise his presence every day
settings.readers: Matthew's Jewish-Christian community, perhaps in Antioch or Galilee, was learning to welcome Gentiles. The ending tells them that mission to all nations is the risen Lord's own command, not a departure from Israel's story.
views: The mission goes to every people, Jews included (Meier, most scholars).
The mission now turns to non-Jews (Hare and Harrington).

traditions.q: The commission says "make... into disciples, baptizing them... teaching them" (28:19–20). Does that order mean only people who have become disciples should be baptized? (The wider question of infant baptism is on the card at 19:14.)
views: Yes. The order is first make disciples, then baptize; baptism is the believer's public act of obedience, by immersion (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 7; Second London Confession 29).

Yes. Baptism is for those who have learned repentance and amendment of life and ask for it (Schleitheim Confession, article 1). The order teach, then baptize, was a central argument of the first Anabaptists.

No. "Make disciples" is the main verb, and baptizing and teaching are how disciples are made, in either order; in a believing household a child is made a disciple through baptism and then taught (Catechism 1250–1252).
No. The command names all nations, and children are part of the nations; baptism is the means by which God makes disciples, and teaching follows (Luther's Large Catechism on Baptism).
No. The participles describe the parts of discipling, not a required sequence, and the children of believers belong to the covenant (Westminster Confession 28.4).

traditions.q: Must baptism be given with the words "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (28:19), and what does the one "name" mean?
views: Yes. The Trinitarian formula with water is essential to valid baptism; Catholics recognize baptisms by other churches given this way (Catechism 1240, 1256).
Yes. Baptism is in the name of the Holy Trinity, with threefold immersion, one for each name.
Trinitarian Pentecostals, such as the Assemblies of God, baptize with the words of 28:19.
Oneness Pentecostals, such as the United Pentecostal Church International, baptize "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38), holding that the one "name" of Father, Son and Spirit in 28:19 is Jesus.

Baptism by immersion uses the words of 28:19 (Doctrine and Covenants 20:73), but the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are understood as three distinct beings, one in purpose. For that reason the Catholic Church ruled in 2001 that these baptisms are not valid, and many other churches also do not recognize them.

Baptism is "in the name of the Father, the Son and the holy spirit," understood as acknowledging Jehovah, his Son Jesus, who is not God Almighty, and the holy spirit as God's active force, not a person.

traditions.q: The women and the eleven "bowed down" before the risen Jesus (28:9, 17), with a Greek word that also means worship. Is Jesus to be worshiped as God?
views: Yes. The Nicene Creed confesses the Son as "true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one essence with the Father," so he receives the same worship as the Father. Orthodox prayer gives it in the doxology, "Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit," and the bowing of the disciples in 28:17 is read as worship of God (Ware, The Orthodox Church).
Yes. Jesus is true God and true man; adoration (latria) is due to him alone with the Father and the Spirit, distinguished from the honor given to saints (Catechism 2096, 2132).
Yes. The Son is "very and eternal God, of one substance and equal with the Father" and is to be worshiped as God (Westminster Confession 8.2, 21.2).
No. The Greek proskyneō can mean bowing in respect; the New World Translation renders it here "did obeisance." Worship in the full sense belongs to Jehovah alone; Jesus is honored as God's Son.
